• Name: European freshwater crab
  • Other names: Levantine freshwater crab
  • Scientific name: Potamon potamios
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Type: Semi-terrestrial
  • Keeping: Easy
  • Breeding: Medium
  • Average carapace size: up to 5–7 cm
  • Average size across the leg span: 10–15 cm
  • Optimal temperature: 22–26°C
  • Optimal humidity: 50–70%
  • Optimal pH: 7.0–8.0
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament: Aggressive
  • Life span: 6+ years
  • Colour: white-dark and purple-to-black pattern

Despite its wide distribution, Potamon potamios is listed on the IUCN Red List as near threatened because of pesticide pollution.

Potamon potamios is primarily distributed in freshwater habitats in Eastern Europe and the Near East. It can be found in various countries, including the Balkans, Greece (mainland and south-eastern Aegean Islands), Russia (southern regions), Cyprus, southern parts of Turkey, Palestine, Syria, Lebanon, northern Iran, Israel (Dead Sea area) and Egypt (Sinai Peninsula).

Potamon potamios is usually found under stones in the shallow water of temperate rivers and streams, where these crabs are adapted to be semi-terrestrial and can dig deep burrows into muddy substrates.

Potamon potamios does not require a lot of space. A 10-gallon (40 litre) tank can house 1 adult crab. One male and one female can be kept together in an enclosure of 15 gallons (60 litres).

Males should not be kept in the same tank because of aggression and territorial fighting.

Stocking is one of the most important factors when keeping crabs. Overcrowding is a major source of stress for crabs. In most cases it leads to health problems, aggression and cannibalism.

Note: Potamon potamios are excellent escape artists. They easily climb vertical surfaces and often use this ability to escape from the tank, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.

Potamon potamios are not fully aquatic animals. Although they spend most of their lives in water, they still have some degree of terrestrial activity, so it is crucial to address their core needs.

Land vs water ratio

Potamon potamios is a semi-terrestrial species. Although these crabs are more aquatic, they do not stay in water all the time. The water area should take at least 70–80% of the space in the tank.

  • These crabs molt (shed their old exoskeleton) in water.
  • In nature, water also provides more hiding places and is generally a safer place.

Water requirements

  • They need only freshwater. Note: experiments showed that Potamon potamios could survive in seawater for at least 2 weeks. Nonetheless, they never voluntarily enter saltwater.
  • The water only needs to be a few inches deep, big enough to completely submerge the crab and nothing more. As long as water pools can completely cover their entire bodies, they will be fine.
  • It should also have some hiding places, since these crabs molt in the water.
  • It is crucial to provide a variety of surfaces for them to get out of the water. Rocks or driftwood can be placed in the water to create small islands the crab can climb onto.

Classic paludarium setup

For a classic paludarium setup, these crabs thrive in water with a pH of at least 7.0–8.0, KH 0–10 and GH 4–16.

Potamon potamios is an omnivore and an opportunistic species.

According to the study, in its feeding habit this species behaves as a generalist, actively preying on frogs, fish and various small invertebrates, as well as scraping alga-covered surfaces or grazing on vegetable debris, mainly dead leaves and plants. Cannibalism occurs between individuals of unequal size.

If kept in paludariums, suggested foods include:

  • leaves,
  • plants,
  • vegetables,
  • crushed snails,
  • earthworms,
  • dead fish or shrimp,
  • frozen bloodworms,
  • detritus worms,
  • tubifex worms,
  • blackworms, etc.
  • Diet type: Omnivorous
  • Food preference: Mix of meats and vegetation
  • Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week for adults; daily for juveniles

Feeding rules in captivity

  • Leave their food for 24 hours before removing it. To prevent water contamination, leftover food should be removed by siphoning before fresh food is added. Leaves can be left in the tank for several days.
  • Leave old exoskeletons. Do not remove molted exoskeletons; the crabs will eat them later.
  • Check their hiding places. Potamon potamios may drag and store food in its hiding spots for later consumption. Check them from time to time to prevent bacterial contamination.
  • Diversity. Crabs need a varied diet. Do not give them the same food all the time; change their diet periodically.

Potamon potamios is not social. On the contrary, it is known for aggressive and territorial behaviour, especially during the breeding season.

These crabs are active, both in water and on land. They are very agile and can be observed moving between aquatic and terrestrial environments in search of food and shelter.

Their semi-aquatic (amphibious) lifestyle allows them to explore a variety of habitats. Males have been noticed to spread easily into the surrounding terrestrial habitats, straying up to 40 m from the stream at night.

While Potamon potamios is primarily nocturnal, it also shows some diurnal behaviour, especially large individuals.

This species can be classified as a secondary burrower. Although it can dig burrows in muddy substrates, it does not rely on them and does not spend all its time there.

  • Social: No
  • Active: Yes
  • Peaceful: No
  • Territorial: Yes
  • Burrowers: Yes

Etymology

The genus name "Potamon" can be traced back to the ancient Greek word "Ποταμόν", which means "flood" or "rapid flow". The species name "Potamios" is derived from the Greek word "Ποταμίος", which means "little or small stream". Overall, the etymology reflects the concept of small fast-flowing rivers and streams.

Taxonomy

These crabs belong to the family Potamidae, which includes freshwater crabs.

  • Kingdom: Animalia
  • Phylum: Arthropoda
  • Subphylum: Crustacea
  • Class: Malacostraca
  • Order: Decapoda
  • Family: Potamidae
  • Genus: Potamon
  • Species: Potamios

Because of their wide distribution in remote areas, there has been limited mixing of the genetic pool of this species, which has allowed numerous subspecies to emerge. Currently, 7 subspecies are considered valid:

  • Potamon potamios ssp. Cyprion Pretzmann, 1962
  • Potamon potamios ssp. Karamani Pretzmann, 1962
  • Potamon potamios ssp. Karpathos Ghiavarini, 1934
  • Potamon potamios ssp. cretaion Ghiavarini, 1934
  • Potamon potamios ssp. Palestinian Bott, 1967
  • Potamon potamios ssp. potamios (Olivier, 1804)
  • Potamon potamios ssp. schoenmanni Pretzmann, 1986 (Naxos Island)

Description

This is a medium-sized crab that usually grows to 5–7 cm (carapace), but in exceptional cases it can reach 10 cm.

Distinguishing characteristics according to the study:

  • Carapace: slightly arched, smooth and concave. The anterior lateral margin of the carapace is well developed and bears numerous very small, rounded teeth.
  • Gonopod: the first gonopod is conical or slender, without a swollen mesial part. The terminal joint of the first gonopod is elongately conical, with the mesial part not curved outwards. The flexible area between the two segments is noticeably double-lobed.
  • Chelipeds: the claws are relatively large and unequal in length. They have high-ridged teeth that leave a gap when closed, set alternately with one larger and three to four smaller knobs.

Interesting fact: the taxonomy of Potamon is based predominantly on characters of the male reproductive organs (the gonopods).

Lifespan

There are currently no studies on the maximum lifespan of these crabs in the wild. In nature they often face risks such as predation, disease and adverse environmental conditions, which can reduce their lifespan.

However, under controlled and optimal conditions, Potamon potamios can live at least 5–6 years in paludariums.

Plant safety

No, they are not plant safe. It is not recommended to keep them in heavily planted tanks. There is a very high chance that they will eat, cut and shred any plant they can reach.

The only viable options for this species are:

  • plastic plants,
  • floating plants,
  • some cheap plants that you are ready to lose.

Calcium

Crabs, like other crustaceans, depend on calcium, particularly during molting. This mineral is necessary for the development and maintenance of the hard exoskeleton, which provides protection and support.

Insufficient calcium intake can lead to weakened shells and deformed limbs. It is therefore crucial for crabs to have a balanced diet that includes sources of calcium, such as algae, or supplements formulated specifically for crabs.
